comment_text:
Mr. Mayor where do you stand on the second amendment and good guys carrying guns? I am a diehard Democrat liberal who believes in the second amendment and the first thing I did when I moved to Florida in February was to get my concealed carry permit, which is not even required down here, but I did it correctly and I passed the background check. I can carry everywhere I go, there are very few restrictions, but I promise you one thing I hope one day you will realize, when good guys have guns, (just like Idaho found out) bad guys will be stopped much sooner. Police cannot be everywhere, we don’t expect them to be everywhere. I am hoping that the Supreme Court finally makes it reciprocal where all states must and I say again must honor all concealed carry permit permits, no matter where you are. I know I’m ranting and it doesn’t have much to do with the terrible tragedy, but I’ve learned that guns aren’t the problem, it’s when the wrong people have them in their hands and we can’t stop everything but we can stop the threat if there’s more good guys around with the ability to do so. Sometimes good guys with guns go astray there’s no doubt about that even police officers when they are off duty at times hurt their families, friends or loved ones. We can’t stop everything but good guys with guns are an extra resource. 

I know that in my lifetime, especially with this conservative court, who I never agree with will eventually recognize gun rights throughout the whole country just like they do with the privilege that is a drivers license. ￼￼

Please tell me one law that anybody in New York or in Washington has enacted that has restricted the police department from removing illegal guns from the streets. First of all, I don’t blame the police department for this, they didn’t know that gun existed and if they did, they would’ve confiscated it, but there are no laws in place that restrict any law-enforcement agencies from taking illegal weapons assuming that their search and seizure is legal.  

Please excuse the mistakes this was dictated to Siri. ￼￼￼

comment_text:
It’s not about the gun! . How about we start to hold the parents accountable?!!!!
If a child is walking around with a firearm and shooting other children, the conversation shouldn’t be with gun laws or the weapon itself. The root cause can include a lack of parental responsibility. Parents who fail to secure their firearms or whose gross negligence allows a minor unsupervised time to access a deadly weapon should be held legally accountable.
At a minimum, prosecutors should consider charges such as child endangerment, reckless conduct, or gross negligence when the evidence supports them. Accountability shouldn’t end with the shooter—responsibility begins at home.

post_text: Mayor Spano calls on lawmakers to address the root causes of gun violence following the fatal shooting on Elm Street.  This is Yonkers’ first homicide in about a year, but one is too many. Every victim, every family and every neighborhood deserves safer streets.
comment_text:
We’re constantly told that overdevelopment will make our neighborhoods safer. But where is the evidence?

What many residents are actually seeing is more reckless driving, cars with modified exhausts, music so loud it shakes our walls, more public disturbances, and more visible drug activity. The problems haven’t disappeared, they’ve simply moved. As Pretty Woman said, “It’s geography.”

Meanwhile, the quality of life keeps slipping away. The Sawmill River is polluted. I reported a scooter bike and other debris in the water to the Parks Department two weeks before the Fourth of July, and as of this weekend, it was still there.

Residents keep reporting potholes, traffic problems, excessive honking, and noise. At the corner of Main Street and Riverdale Avenue, people constantly honk because there isn’t a clearly posted “Right Turn on Red” sign. It’s a simple issue that could easily be addressed.

Instead of focusing on basic quality of life, all we see is more overdevelopment and the destruction of what made Yonkers unique. Historic buildings, mature trees, murals, and green spaces disappear while new construction goes up.

And where is the accountability? At 87 Nepperhan Avenue, demolition took place without any visible dust mitigation despite concerns about dust and possible hazardous materials. Ironically, the Mayor’s own videos documented the conditions.

Residents deserve clean streets, clean parks, safer roads, responsible development, and a city government that addresses everyday problems, not just approves more buildings.
author: Sophie Cahen Vorburger

post_text: Mayor Spano calls on lawmakers to address the root causes of gun violence following the fatal shooting on Elm Street.  This is Yonkers’ first homicide in about a year, but one is too many. Every victim, every family and every neighborhood deserves safer streets.
comment_text:
Mayor Spano,

Please do not turn this into a political issue. Instead of placing blame everywhere else, we need to focus on where responsibility begins.

A 15-year-old should not be able to get access to a gun. That raises an important question: Where are the parents? Responsibility and accountability start at home. Children need guidance, structure, discipline, and values from the adults raising them.

Schools also play an important role by reinforcing expectations, teaching responsibility, and maintaining consequences for harmful behavior. When young people grow up without structure or accountability at home, the effects often show up in the classroom and on our streets.

Parents who fail to properly supervise or guide their children should be held accountable when their neglect contributes to these situations. We need to address the root causes by promoting responsibility, accountability, and stronger support for families and schools, rather than making this another political debate.
author: Gerri Fico Kelly

post_text: Mayor Spano calls on lawmakers to address the root causes of gun violence following the fatal shooting on Elm Street.  This is Yonkers’ first homicide in about a year, but one is too many. Every victim, every family and every neighborhood deserves safer streets.
comment_text:
Stop the Finger-Pointing. Start Taking Responsibility.

A 15-year-old with a gun. Think about that for a second. How does someone that young get their hands on a firearm?

Then there’s another question that doesn’t get asked enough: It happened around midnight. Where were his parents? We need to have an honest conversation about parental responsibility, too. If more kids were home at a reasonable hour instead of out in the middle of the night, maybe they wouldn’t be exposed to the violence happening on our streets.

Every time a tragedy like this happens, the political blame game begins. The mayor blames Republicans. Others blame Democrats. But many of the elected officials in Washington, the state, the county, and the city are endorsed by this very mayor. So what are they doing to solve the problem?

Enough with the press conferences and political talking points. If leaders truly believe this is a public safety emergency, then treat it like one. Call an emergency meeting. Bring everyone to the table. Work across party lines and pass meaningful legislation that addresses violent crime, illegal guns, youth intervention, and accountability.

The public doesn’t care who gets the political win. We care about making our neighborhoods safer and preventing the next tragedy.

It’s time to stop using these heartbreaking moments as opportunities to score political points. Leadership isn’t about assigning blame after another child is shot. Leadership is about taking responsibility before the next child is.
author: The Yonkers Watchdog

A LETTER TO THE CLASS OF 2027… AND EVERY STUDENT WHO FOLLOWS

https://linktr.ee/THEWEALTHLABYO

This may be the most important letter I’ve ever written.

Not because it’s about me.

Because it’s about you.

It’s about every student wondering if what they’re learning today will actually help them tomorrow.

Let’s be honest…

Schools taught many of us how to find the square root—but not always how to read a credit report.

We learned about the Boston Tea Party—but not always why overdraft fees can empty a bank account.

Somewhere along the way, life became the teacher… and tuition became expensive.

That doesn’t have to be the story for the Class of 2027.

This letter is my promise that your future matters enough to fight for, prepare for and invest in.

Whether you’re a student, parent, grandparent, educator, coach or community leader, this letter belongs to you too.

Because every generation has one responsibility:

Leave the next generation better prepared than we were.

Take a few minutes.

Read the letter.

Talk about it.

Challenge it.

Most importantly, ask the young people in your life one question:

“What kind of future do you want?”

Their answer may change all of ours.

Welcome to THE W.E.A.L.T.H. LAB.

WELCOME TO AUGUST. WELCOME TO THE W.E.A.L.T.H. LAB.

A new month has arrived.

Some people see another page on the calendar.

We see another chance to prepare the next generation for the one test life gives everyone—adulthood.

Because adulthood doesn’t ask whether you memorized the answers on a worksheet.

It asks whether you know how to earn, save, budget, borrow wisely, invest, build, recover, and leave something better than you found it.

August is where teachers prepare.
Students wonder.
Parents hope.
Communities reset.

And somewhere, a future graduate is one lesson away from changing the trajectory of an entire family.

Here’s the good news:
You don’t have to know everything.

You just have to be willing to learn.

(And yes… if your bank account could talk, it would probably ask why you bought that thing you swore was “on sale.” Financial literacy has a sense of humor, too.)

At THE W.E.A.L.T.H. LAB, we believe education should prepare students not only for graduation—but for rent, taxes, credit, entrepreneurship, investing, opportunity, setbacks, and the confidence to navigate all of it.

This isn’t just about money.

It’s about freedom.
Responsibility.
Choices.
Legacy.

Welcome to August.

Let’s make this the month we stop preparing students only for exams—and start preparing them for life.

Class is in session. The future is waiting. FUND THE REQUIREMENT. FUND THE FUTURE.

WELCOME TO AUGUST. WELCOME TO THE W.E.A.L.T.H. LAB.

A new month has arrived.

Some people see another page on the calendar.

We see another chance to prepare the next generation for the one test life gives everyone—adulthood.

Students wonder.
Parents hope.
Communities reset.

Responsibility.
Choices.
Legacy.

Welcome to August.

Let’s make this the month we stop preparing students only for exams—and start preparing them for life.

Class is in session. The future is waiting. FUND THE REQUIREMENT. FUND THE FUTURE.
